title: Built a racing manager. My son is the beta tester.
author: salsa2k
selftext:
I had the idea in July, spent the summer researching and planning, and started coding in mid-September. Two months and about 1,700 commits later, Pulse Racer is in a free open beta on itch.io.

My beta tester is my 9-year-old son. We race together every day, and most days I end up adjusting something: balance, track decorations, or small touches like the crowd opening umbrellas on a rainy race day.

**The game:** think of a much simpler motorsport manager. Your car drives itself. You pick tires, set your driver's pace, call the pit stop and, above all, time your PULSE boost. The bet is on simplicity: quick races you can jump into, against real players and AI drivers, on circuits, rally stages and rallycross tracks.



**Where AI comes in:**

* **Code:** Claude Code, plus some OpenAI Codex. The client is Godot 4 with typed GDScript; the server is Go.
* **Rules live in docs, not prompts:** every game rule is a markdown doc in the repo. An AGENTS.md tells the agents to read the relevant doc before touching code, and to update the doc first when a decision changes. Repeatable jobs (building a circuit from a reference image, dressing a rally stage, preparing a release) are agent skills.
* **Audio:** ElevenLabs for the race engineer radio, the presenter voice, some sound effects and the music.
* **Art:** textures, logo, UI icons and some 3D models were made with AI help and finished in Blender. I tried Tripo AI for 3D and didn't have much luck, so some models, like the cars, are bought asset packs.
* **Localization:** 12 languages translated with AI. I reviewed English and Portuguese myself (I'm a native Portuguese speaker living in Canada); the others haven't had a native review yet.



**Built to stay cheap:**

* Fully server-authoritative: the Go server runs every race, and the client just shows it.
* A main server orchestrates small, low-cost race workers. If one goes down, only the races on that node are affected.
* SQLite, for simplicity. It's more than enough for now, and I can migrate to another database later if I need to.
* The goal is to keep hosting costs very low without hurting gameplay.



**What I learned:**

* Agents follow written rules really well, but they don't remember last week's decisions. Writing every decision down fixed most of the drift.
* Every UI change starts as a mockup I approve before any code gets written.



**Where it's at:** the plan is to launch on Steam, and I've been waiting almost a month for my Steam app ID. Until then, the free open beta on itch.io is how I collect player feedback and bug reports. Press F9 anywhere in the game to send one; a screenshot is attached automatically. The beta runs on Windows and macOS and needs internet and an itch.io account (you sign in from the game). Progress gets wiped when the beta ends.

* Beta: [https://rafinha.itch.io/pulse-racer](https://rafinha.itch.io/pulse-racer)
* YouTube, with trailers, gameplay, and shorts: [https://www.youtube.com/@PulseRacerGame](https://www.youtube.com/@PulseRacerGame)



I'm happy to answer questions about the agent setup or the architecture, and any feedback on the game is welcome.

comments.author: Xinnobun
comments.body: "Six Drivers. One Track. Only one winner." is the worst opening hook to a trailer I've ever heard in my life. For a racing game, you may as well say the sky is blue.

replies.author: salsa2k
replies.body: That's the point, it's a nod to the old "In a world..." movie trailers. Cheesy on purpose.

comments.author: Timely-Tradition-471
comments.body:
Hey! I'm Joshua, part of the U.S. team at Tripo Studio. First off, congrats on getting Pulse Racer into open beta! It's really cool seeing how you've approached building the game, especially involving your son in the testing process and making adjustments based on that day-to-day feedback.

I also appreciate you sharing your experience with Tripo. I'd be curious to learn a bit more about what you were trying to create and where things fell short. We're continuously improving our 3D generation and workflows, and hearing directly from developers building actual games is incredibly valuable.

I'd love to connect, check out more of your work, and hear about your experience with the tools you used throughout development. Wishing you the best with the beta!

replies.author: salsa2k
replies.body:
Hi Joshua,

I should correct my post a bit. I did end up using Tripo for three models in the game: the driver, the pit crew members and one formula car. All three needed a lot of work in Blender afterwards (mostly through Blender MCP), but they started in Tripo. So “didn’t have much luck” was a bit unfair. It’s more that the hit rate was low for what I needed.

  
Here’s the honest feedback:

My process. I made reference images with ChatGPT from 4 angles (front, side, back, top), with neutral colors, no shadows and as little detail as possible, to give the model the cleanest input I could. Even so, the results were hit or miss. Out of all the cars I tried, I kept just one formula car, and I still had to fix it in Blender.

Failed generations on a small plan. On the entry tier, 3 or 4 retries in a row came out completely wrong. In one case the car was fully inverted, even after I changed the prompt and the references. When you’re on a low tier and watching every credit, paying for several unusable results in a row is really frustrating. A cheap low-res preview before the full generation, or credits back for clearly broken outputs, would help a lot.

Credit math on the pricing page. The Pro plan says “up to 100 models”, but as far as I can tell that’s only for basic generations. Once you use Smart Mesh and texturing, the real number drops a lot. I only found that out after subscribing. Showing the cost per feature, like “\~X models with Smart Mesh + textures”, would set clearer expectations.

What worked. The characters were a good starting point. The proportions and the base mesh saved me time compared with modeling from scratch, even with the cleanup afterwards.
